title: GO2 Health medical clinic in Brisbane waited almost three months to alert patients it was hacked
full_text:
Another medical clinic has revealed it has been targeted by hackers, less than a week after Partnered Health announced a major data breach.
GO2 Health in Everton Park, in Brisbane's north, said the clinic's main email mailbox was accessed in April after a phishing attack.
It wasn't until almost three months later that affected patients were notified.
A spokesperson for the clinic, which offers general practice and veteran care services, said they engaged experts to contain the breach and altered staff who use the mailbox on April 24.
"Unfortunately, our investigation did ultimately identify that some data within the mailbox may have been accessed, including some patients' Department of Veteran's Affairs ID Numbers and other information that our patients may have provided the inbox," they said.
"Importantly, there was no access to the system where we primarily store patient information, and the mailbox uses an auto-archive, so the data accessed only pertains to emails sent during the previous 12 months leading up to the incident."
Businesses which store private information, such as medical clinics, are required to alert the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) within 30 days if they believe the breach is "likely to result in serious harm".
GO2 Health alerted the OAIC on May 18, but affected patients did not receive an email until July 16.
The clinic said it took them nearly three months to identify which patients had their emails accessed.
"We wanted to avoid causing undue concern and confusion by notifying the wrong people, or communicating inaccurate information," the spokesperson said.
'Precious time' lost
Amanda* is one of those who received an alert from GO2 Health.
She said while she understands the argument against sending out a mass alert, three months is too long.
"I think they've wasted really precious time for people to check their accounts and change their passwords," she said.
"[Those affected] have missed that opportunity to be a little more vigilant."
As a veteran who is receiving psychological treatment, Amanda said a lot of "extremely personal and extremely sensitive" information relating to her care was sent to the mailbox in question.
"It's very upsetting to know that's potentially going to end up on the web somewhere, and who knows what might be done with it in the future.
"I know the clinic processes a lot of DVA claims for people, so I can only imagine there would be a massive volume of personal information that's sitting in that mailbox over a 12-month period."
Experts have called for tighter regulations on medical companies which fall victim to cyber attacks, requiring them to have to notify patients early in the investigation process.
This is especially important, they argue, given the sensitive nature of the information clinics hold.
Partnered Health, which had 16 of its nearly 60 clinics hacked in June, waited 22 days before notifying affected patients.
Amanda has applied to change her Medicare number and said she had reached out to GO2 Health to ask if she needed to also update her Department of Veterans Affairs card but hasn't heard back.
In a digital world, she said clinics needed to treat patient data with "more respect".
"I'm still going to be needing to receive treatments, but I think I'm going to be more cautious and ask more questions around how my data is stored."
*not her real name.
